_needsNewUnit.2Pf.01, 2Pf.03: Forces changing the movement of an object, and the rule that a thing only speeds up, slows down or changes direction when something else causes it. 2Pf.02 (forces changing an object's SHAPE) is closed here, inside Changing Materials, because squashing and bending a material is what that unit is about. Movement is not: the nearest units are Rocks and The Earth and the Sun, and force teaching in either would be filler. Grade 1 Unit 5 (Pushes and Pulls) teaches this content a year early and Grade 3 Unit 5 (Forces and Magnets) a year late, so a learner who takes the course in order does meet it twice - it is Stage 2 that cannot claim it. concepts.title: Bodies, Skin and Teeth
concepts.explanation:
Animals need the same things you need, and their bodies are built to get them - but not all in the same way.

Compare yourself with a goat. You both have a head, eyes, a nose, a mouth and four limbs. But you have arms with hands, and the goat has four legs with hooves. You walk upright; the goat walks on all four.

Now look at what covers them. Your body is covered in skin, with hair on your head. A goat is covered in hair all over. A hen is covered in feathers. A fish is covered in scales. A frog has smooth, damp skin. The covering is one of the quickest ways to tell one kind of animal from another.

Open your mouth in a mirror. Your front teeth are flat and sharp at the edge - incisors, for biting into a piece of bread or an apple. Further back your teeth are wide and bumpy - molars, for grinding food up small. The pointed ones between them are canines, for holding and tearing.

A goat has wide grinding teeth and no sharp tearing teeth, because it eats only plants. A cat has long pointed teeth, because it eats meat. The teeth tell you what an animal eats.

Teeth do not grow back once your adult ones are through, so brushing them morning and night is looking after something you will use for the rest of your life.

Brushing your teeth is one part of a bigger job: keeping your whole body healthy, which is called managing your health. Three things matter most. Diet is what you eat - a mix of foods like ugali, beans, vegetables, fruit and milk gives your body everything it needs to grow and mend itself, where eating only one kind of food does not. Hygiene means keeping yourself clean: washing your hands before you eat and after the toilet, bathing, and brushing your teeth all stop tiny germs from making you ill. And moving your body every day - running, playing, walking to fetch water - keeps your heart and muscles strong, the same way using a tool keeps it from rusting. Diet, hygiene and exercise are three separate habits, and a healthy body needs all three, not just one.
concepts.example: Look in a mirror with your mouth open. Find a flat front tooth and a wide back tooth. Say what each one is for. Then think of an animal you know and say whether its teeth are for grinding plants or tearing meat.

concepts.title: When a Body Is Unwell
concepts.explanation:
Living things need food, water, air and shelter. When something goes wrong inside a body, we say it is ill.

Being ill is not the same as being hurt. If you fall and cut your knee, you are injured - you can see exactly what happened and where. Illness works from the inside, and often you cannot see any cause at all.

There are signs to look for, and you already know most of them. A hot forehead, called a fever. A cough. A headache. A stomach ache. Feeling tired when you have not been working. Not wanting to eat. Sometimes being sick.

Those signs are useful, because they are how you tell someone what is wrong. A nurse cannot see inside you either; she asks what hurts, feels whether you are hot, and listens.

Most illness passes with rest, clean water and time. Some needs medicine, and some needs a clinic. The important thing at your age is to tell a grown-up as soon as you feel one of those signs, rather than waiting to see.
concepts.example: Name three signs that tell you somebody is ill rather than injured. Then say what you should do first if you wake up with a hot forehead and a headache.

concepts.title: Growing Up, and Your Family Face
concepts.explanation:
Every animal that has young starts small and changes as it gets older.

A newborn kid can barely stand. Its legs are wobbly, it drinks only milk, and it stays close to its mother. Months later it is steady on its feet, it eats grass, and it goes off on its own. Years later it is a full-grown goat with young of its own.

A hen's chick is a ball of soft down that cannot fly. It grows proper feathers, gets bigger and heavier, and becomes a hen or a cockerel.

You are doing the same thing. As a baby you could not walk, talk or feed yourself, and your teeth had not come through. Look at a photograph of yourself as a baby and then look in a mirror: taller, stronger, and able to do a hundred things you could not do then.

Now look at the rest of your family. You may have your mother's eyes and your father's nose, or hair like your grandmother's. Young animals are the same - a black goat and a brown goat can have a kid with patches of both.

Young are never an exact copy of one parent. They carry a mixture of features from both, which is why brothers and sisters look alike and are still easy to tell apart.
concepts.example: Find or think of a photograph of yourself as a baby. Name two things you could not do then that you can do now. Then name one feature you share with someone else in your family, and say who.

concepts.title: A Force Can Change a Shape
concepts.explanation:
Heating and cooling change materials. So does something much simpler: a push or a pull.

A push or a pull is called a force. You use them all day without naming them - pressing, squeezing, pulling, bending.

Take a lump of soft clay or dough. Press it with your thumb and a dent appears. Roll it and it becomes a sausage. Squash it flat and it becomes a disc. It is the same clay all the way through; only the shape has changed, because your hand pushed it.

A force can change the shape of harder things too, if it is strong enough. Squeeze a ripe tomato and it dents. Bend a thin stick and it curves. Stretch a rubber band and it grows longer and thinner.

Some shapes go back on their own and some do not. Let go of the rubber band and it springs back. Let go of the clay and the dent stays.

So there are two ways to change a material in this unit: change its temperature, or push and pull it into a new shape.

A force can change something else too, beyond shape: it can change how an object MOVES. Kick a ball and it was still, then a push makes it speed up and roll away. Roll that same ball across sand and it slows down and stops by itself - except it is not really by itself: the sand rubbing against it is a force too, and that force is what slows it down. Push a rolling ball from the side and it does not keep going the same way, it curves off in the new direction the push sent it.

Notice the rule hiding in all three. A moving thing never speeds up, slows down, stops or changes direction on its own - something else always has to cause the change, whether that something is a kick, a hand, or just the ground rubbing against it. A ball rolling on smooth, hard ground keeps going much further than the same ball rolling on sand, because there is less rubbing to slow it down. Left alone, with nothing pushing or pulling on it at all, a moving thing simply carries on moving as it is.
concepts.example: Take a small piece of dough or wet soil, and a rubber band. Change the shape of each with a push or a pull. Say which one went back to its old shape when you let go, and which one kept the new shape.
